item.title: Beyond the Visible-Invisible Disability Binary
item.description:
Bias

Beyond the Visible-Invisible Disability Binary

Introducing the disability observability spectrum.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • A new framework shows disability occurs on an observability spectrum instead of a visible/invisible binary.
  • More observed disabilities trigger paternalistic ableism characterized by pity.
  • Less observed disabilities trigger ableism in the form of delegitimization and suspicion.

For too long, we’ve relied on a simple binary to describe disability: Is it visible or invisible, concealable or not? Although these terms are common, they don’t quite capture the fluid, multisensory nature of disability. In a new publication, Marine Granjon, Pauline Rasset, and I propose a new framework. Instead of a binary, we propose the disability observability spectrum.

The most common term we use, “visibility,” is ocularcentric—it prioritizes sight as the only way to perceive difference, ignoring other sensory channels like sound. For instance, you might not see a speech disorder, but you may hear it. "Concealment" is an active behavior, not a permanent state. Not everyone with a concealable disability chooses to hide it, nor should they.

This is why I use the term "observability spectrum.” The verb form—"observed"—shifts the focus away from the individual and places it squarely on the social interaction. Whether a disability is observed isn't inherent to the condition; it's a dynamic interaction that depends on the individual, the observer, and the context.

What Moves Us Along the Spectrum?

Whether a disability is observed at any point in time depends on a combination of factors within the individual, the observer, and the context.

The Individual: The prototypicality of a disability—that is, the extent to which the disability type aligns with public stereotypes about what a disability is—affects whether it is observed. A wheelchair user is the international symbol of disability, appearing on accessible bathroom stalls and parking spaces. Contrasted with a less prototypical disability like facial paralysis, individuals using wheelchairs are more likely to be recognized as disabled.

A disability may not directly affect the person’s appearance but may involve the use of assistive tools or service animals that nonetheless make the disability observable. For example, you probably can’t look at someone and know they have epilepsy most of the time, but if they get a service dog to alert them to seizure activity, their disability would then be observable.

Disability course—whether symptoms change over time—influences observability. Someone with multiple sclerosis may be observed as disabled during a flare when using a scooter, but not when they are walking unaided during remission.

The Observer: Not all observers notice the same things. Someone with “insider knowledge"—perhaps because they have a disability themselves or know someone who does—might notice subtle cues that others miss.

The Context: Our environment changes everything. Inaccessible spaces make a disability more observable. A wheelchair user’s disability might not be observed during a Zoom job interview, but it becomes observed the moment they arrive for an in-person meeting.

The Observability Spectrum Influences Ableism Pathways

Where a person falls on the observability spectrum predicts the specific “flavor” of ableism they are likely to encounter. By integrating this spectrum with key psychology theories, we can map out distinct pathways to ableism: paternalism or delegitimization.

The disability observability spectrum predicts specific stereotypes, prejudices, and discriminatory behaviors depending on the extent to which a disability is observed.
Source: Kathleen Bogart

Paternalistic Pathway (Observable Side of the Spectrum)

The Stereotype Content Model theorizes that we form stereotypes about people based on two dimensions: their perceived warmth (e.g., friendliness and trustworthiness) and their perceived competence (e.g., capability and independence). When a disability is readily observed, people tend to stereotype the individual as warm but incompetent.

Building on this theory, the Behaviors from Intergroup Affect and Stereotypes (BIAS) Map indicates stereotypes trigger a specific set of emotions and behaviors. Stereotypes of warmth and incompetence lead people to feel pity toward those with more observed disabilities, which leads to paternalistic behaviors like unsolicited help and assumptions of inability. One study found that people with observable disabilities were six times more likely to be subjected to unwanted help than those with nonobservable disabilities.

Delegitimization Pathway (Less Observable Side of the Spectrum)

Recent research suggests this pattern is reversed toward people with less observed disabilities—they are perceived as more competent but colder than those with observed disabilities. These stereotypes are associated with feelings of distrust and suspicion toward those with less observed disabilities. People in this category are twice as likely as those with observable disabilities to face accusations of “faking it” to exploit the system.

Zone of Ambiguity

What about those who do not fall neatly into the visible/invisible binary? When disabilities fall in the middle of the observability spectrum, they land in a zone of ambiguity. Consider the example of narcolepsy, which is not a prototypical disability and involves symptoms that can wax and wane. If a person with narcolepsy falls asleep in class, observers may not attribute it to a disability. They may be incorrectly written off as a bored or lazy student.

Real-World Consequences

Whether a person’s disability falls in the paternalism pathway, the delegitimization pathway, or somewhere in between has important implications for daily life.

The extent to which a disability is observed predicts real world consequences.
Source: Kathleen Bogart
  • Identity. People on the observable side of the spectrum are more likely to identify as disabled and form a positive disability identity. In contrast, people on the other end of the spectrum may internalize the invalidation they experience, believing that they don’t “count” as disabled.
  • Salience to the public: People whose disabilities are less observed experience civil inattention—the privacy afforded to nonstigmatized people in public spaces—and “passing privilege.” Yet, this can feel like erasure of a part of one’s experience or identity. In contrast, those whose disabilities are observed are hypervisible—they will be recognized and remembered in public.
  • Perception of symptoms: Those with more observable disabilities may experience disability spread, a bias where people wrongly assume a disability impacts more domains than it actually does. When people assume that a person who uses a wheelchair also has intellectual disability, that’s disability spread. On the nonobservable end of the spectrum, others may minimize symptoms and their impact.
  • Accommodations: Access to accommodations in the workplace or school may also diverge according to the extent to which the disability is observed. Those whose disabilities are not observed may be denied accommodations, are expected to provide a higher burden of proof, and when accommodations are given, they may be insufficient. Those whose disabilities are observed may experience paternalism in the form of low expectations or overprotection.
  • Healthcare: People on the less observed end of the spectrum frequently face invalidation in medical settings. For many of these disabilities, medical tests or biomarkers are not available. They may be subconsciously threatening to healthcare providers because they are more difficult to assess and treat with the tools provided in their training. On the other end of the spectrum, diagnostic overshadowing—when a healthcare provider wrongly attributes symptoms to an existing disability rather than investigating other causes—occurs for people whose disabilities are observed.

By moving beyond the binary, we can start to address the specific ways ableism manifests in daily life. Paternalism and delegitimization are different ableism pathways rooted in the same observability spectrum. Recognizing this spectrum is the first step toward creating research, policies, and environments that respond to our needs with respect and validation, rather than pity or suspicion.

A version of this article was also published on Substack.

item.title: Looking Inward Won’t Make You Authentic
item.description:
Authenticity

Looking Inward Won’t Make You Authentic

True selfhood is about transcending the ego.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Authenticity isn't found through isolated introspection but contributing to something greater than yourself.
  • Overcoming self-absorption requires connecting both horizontally and vertically.
  • The true self is an active daily practice of presence, humility, and love.

Living authentically was central to existentialism long before it became diluted by modern self-help culture. Today, authenticity is often framed as a solo journey—something achieved merely by turning inward, analyzing our feelings, and uncovering a hidden "core self." But this hyper-focus on introspection often leads to an accidental trap: endless self-absorption disguised as self-discovery.

Philosopher Charles Guignon directly challenges this isolationist view. In On Being Authentic (2004), he writes, “When the ideal of authenticity is understood in its concrete social reality, it becomes clear that being authentic is not simply a matter of focusing on oneself, but also of considering how one’s engagement contributes to the common good of the public world of which one is a part.”

Guignon does not reject the desire to live authentically; rather, he redefines it so that it is not reduced to pure introspection or self-optimization. For authenticity to become real, we must step outside our own heads and engage responsibly with the world around us.

The authentic person is therefore not merely true to their own feelings but also seeks to contribute to something greater than themselves. At this point—something greater than oneself—an interesting connection to the existentialist Søren Kierkegaard emerges.

For Kierkegaard, too, human beings must move beyond the self-absorption that traps the self in despair. But where Guignon describes this larger context as the democratic and social community, Kierkegaard describes it as God.

The difference is crucial: For Guignon, the connection is horizontal—anchored in social, cultural, and democratic space. For Kierkegaard, the connection is vertical. God is not merely a social framework or a cultural construction but the absolute power. While Guignon’s model offers a meaningful way of being-in-the-world through community, Kierkegaard insists that we can overcome despair only by relating to what transcends the purely earthly.

Yet, both thinkers share a vital insight: The self does not exist in isolation; it is shaped and sustained in relation to something larger than the individual. For Kierkegaard, however, this does not mean God can be reduced to a psychological resource. Faith is not a tool to bolster the ego but precisely what shatters human narcissism, leading us to gradually surrender the notion of a fixed self. If faith is known by its fruits, the believer is typically humble, merciful, and kind.

Three Levels of Selfhood

According to Kierkegaard, the human being is spirit. He views spirit as the self, but this self is more than a static synthesis of body and soul, the finite and the infinite. The self is dynamic and processual; it is a relation that relates itself to itself. The self relates to its own existence while recognizing that it has been established by another: God. In the movement from the false to the true self, we can distinguish three levels:

  1. The Dualist Self: Here, the individual guards their distinctiveness. Identity functions like outerwear—social, cultural, or personal markers used to separate oneself from others through status, pride, and ego. This level traps us in division.
  2. The Connected Self: Here, one learns to simply be human. Differences dissolve into the realization that we all share a fundamental vulnerability. The self experiences its connection to the neighbor, making individual well-being inextricably linked to the well-being of the other.
  3. The True Self: Here, the ego steps back to make space for a relationship with God. Kierkegaard makes clear that humanity and God remain distinct—it is a relationship—but through love, one can experience powerful moments of harmony with the sacred.

The Role of Faith

For Kierkegaard, faith is not a classic utopia pointing toward a perfect future. It is better understood as a “here-and-now” utopia. Faith directs us to the present moment, to the neighbor, and to concrete life. It is an ongoing practice—“none of us is the pure Human Being,” Kierkegaard writes in Works of Love.

The Christian, the Dane stresses, is not exempt from living in a world full of social differences, “but by conquering the temptation of diversity, he becomes a Christian.” Becoming a Christian is not an intellectual realization, but a lived action. When the individual discovers the eternal in life, there is no longer room for evasions, excuses, or distance regarding what one “in this now, in this second, in this holy moment must do: then he is on his way to becoming a Christian.”

If we truly loved our neighbor as ourselves, our relationship with the world would radically transform. Faith in God as love helps us move beyond self-absorption. Faith is revealed not through dogmatic certainty or moral perfection but through unconditional surrender to love. The motivation for faith is found in the fruits of love we all recognize: kindness, forgiveness, compassion, and mercy.

Some might ask whether a person can be authentic without being “saved.” Guignon would likely answer yes. Kierkegaard, by contrast, would contend that even the most authentic person in the world remains in despair if the self does not rest transparently in its divine foundation, a higher power or ultimate reality.

Still, the contradiction is less absolute than it first appears. Authenticity may not be the opposite of salvation, but a preparation for it. When we move beyond narcissism and constant self-realization, an opening emerges toward something greater: a movement from the dualist self toward the interconnected, processual self. Authenticity then becomes a clearing of space—a way of rendering us receptive to love and true presence.

Despair is often directed toward tomorrow and anxiety toward finitude, whereas faith is always anchored in the present. Death is constantly present because human beings, as temporal creatures, bloom and wither. Yet many live absent from their own lives, trapped in busyness, performance, and exhausting comparisons. Kierkegaard’s thought reminds us that it is not too late to truly live. When we strip away the masks—status, success, and social roles—we can see the neighbor clearly and recognize that “every human being is the neighbor.”

In this experience lies hope: that a more loving and present life is still possible.

item.title: A Guide to College Homesickness and How to Move Through It
item.description:
Education

A Guide to College Homesickness and How to Move Through It

Homesickness is common in first-years but it can occur at any time in college.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Seventy percent of first-year students feel homesick.
  • The timing and form of homesickness vary widely and include physical, emotional, and cognitive aspects.
  • Practical steps—like naming the feeling and building routines—can help homesickness pass.

In my 20 years as a college mental health counselor, I had many student clients who started their college career in crisis. They had a particularly tough time leaving the comfort and warmth of their families. College seemed like a place of fear and impossibility.

Source: Mia Nosanow

That’s the bad news. The good news is that all of these students ended up developing coping skills for tough times, finding new people that they could hang out with and trust, and in general succeeding in school and life in ways they could not foresee during their first weeks at school.

However we want to label this—homesickness, adjustment disorder, social anxiety—leaving for college is a major transition. While most would agree it is widespread in the first few months of college, I saw this arise for students at all times during their college career. It could be a delayed reaction for second-years, loss of close friends to study abroad their junior year, or a realization they can’t replicate the home they came from during their senior year.

Source: Mia Nosanow

Homesickness is very common

Leaving home for the first time is the usual cause for distress. Studies have shown that 70 percent of first-year students experience some type of homesickness symptoms.

Homesickness presents in a variety of ways

Each person will have their particular way of expressing homesickness.

  • Some will focus on the emotional aspect, feeling loneliness, anxiety, sadness, or irritability.
  • Some will center on the cognitive features, such as being unable to focus, low motivation, or obsessively thinking about home and the past.
  • Some folks might feel numb and shut down, and reveal their homesickness through physical symptoms such as sleep disruption, appetite shifts, headaches, or gastrointestinal distress.
  • And some will choose to cope with unhealthy behaviors such as isolating from others and excessive use of alcohol, gambling, or shopping.

Six healthy steps for coping with homesickness

  1. Name the feelings or behaviors as homesickness. Frequent reminders that this is a common, normal experience will help.
  2. Get support from trusted family and friends. They will likely repeat that homesickness is common and normal and will dissipate with time. They will help focus on building community at school, rather than escaping the situation.
  3. Create new connections and social relationships on campus. This will not happen overnight. It takes a lot of baby steps and shared experiences to make new friends.
  4. Find places on campus that you enjoy and feel more comfortable in. This will take some time and experimentation.
  5. Attend campus events. This creates a sense of belonging that grows with participation.
  6. Build new routines for things that were easy at home, such as meals, sleep schedule, laundry, and where to study. It takes trial and error, but I noticed that the sense of routine kicks in around week three and starts to give relief to students.

How to keep balance with home and school

It has become so easy to stay connected to family and friends who are far away. It is a good thing to stay connected; however, too much of a good thing can get in the way of building new relationships and belonging habits on campus. There is no perfect rule for this, but having some boundaries with how much time is spent on social media, phone calls/texts, and gaming will be helpful. It takes trial and error and bravery to build a new community.

When to seek help

Symptoms of homesickness, such as sadness and isolation, can lead to more serious problems when left unchecked. It's important to reach out to a counselor or health care provider for any of these symptoms (not a complete list):

  • Changes in usual communication habits
  • Changes with eating, sleeping, or class attendance
  • Expressing thoughts of hopelessness
  • Isolation and lack of engagement with opportunities to meet people

While it can seem like the height of crisis when it is first experienced, it’s important to remember that homesickness usually ebbs when students can build new routines and community. It helps to take the long view that campus will soon feel like a second home.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Bearing Children in a Fractured World
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Bearing Children in a Fractured World

Personal Perspective: Reflections as the 9/11 anniversary approaches.

Posted September 10, 2026

How can I bring children into this world? The question surfaced in my mind as the attacks on the World Trade Center unfolded on that impossibly clear morning of September 11, 2001. Just one day earlier, I had learned I was pregnant with my third child. Hours earlier, I had been filled with uncomplicated joy, imagining our growing family, wondering whether this baby might be a daughter after two boys. I hadn’t yet worried about the logistics of caring for three small children with only two arms. I hadn’t thought about how we would fit another child into our tiny studio apartment, which we jokingly referred to as a ten-room studio. I wasn’t thinking about work-life balance or my own health. I was simply elated.

But as the world experienced an inconceivable rupture, that joy was pierced by a sudden, personal terror. Hearing about the first airplane, then the second striking the towers, and finally the realization that this was a coordinated attack, the sense of shock deepened with each unfolding moment. With it, the thought of bringing new life into a world that could fracture so violently became overwhelming, almost frightening.

This was not the first time I had questioned the act of bringing children into the world, and I am far from the first to ask it. Across centuries, thinkers and texts have returned to this same unsettling thought, from Sophocles’ stark claim that “not to be born is best of all,” to Ecclesiastes lament (4:2-3) “And I praise the dead who have already died, above the living, who are yet alive. But better than both is he who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun".

In New York City, conversations about children are often practical and transactional: focused on the cost of raising them, the scarcity of space, the policies meant to support families, and the political promises made to young and struggling parents. At the same time, in many communities, including my own, family is held up as a moral anchor, the highest ideal. Yet the deeper, more ambivalent questions about parenthood are rarely voiced. Within these unspoken assumptions, having a family is expected, and doubts about whether to bring children into the world feel private, even isolating. In the shadow of that day’s events, knowing that life was already forming within me, this long-suppressed question returned with force: why bring children into a world capable of such profound human cruelty?

Like the rest of New Yorkers that day, I felt the pull homeward and realized it was time to relieve the sitter, to make sure we were safe, and to be together. When I arrived, I was grateful that we had chosen not to have a television. Our children were still very young, but deeply observant, and I wanted to avoid, if at all possible, the impossible task of explaining acts of terror to them.

Being with our boys calmed me. I avoided graphic news and conversations with neighbors and other parents, conversations filled with anxious speculation about food shortages or complaints about disrupted holiday travel plans. I yearned for isolation with my family. Perhaps my own past experiences with terror had grounded me, preparing me to respond differently. My thoughts were elsewhere.

Playing with our children, reading silly books, and building train sets became the best antidote to my fear. Their untroubled joy offered a glimpse of something better: possibility, continuity, a future not yet shaped by violence. As we spent those enclosed days together, I began to wonder whether I was projecting my fears onto them, whether I was becoming overprotective.

I realized that my question about bringing new life into the world was rooted in the intense responsibility of parenthood, the instinct to protect, to ensure that children grow healthy in body and mind. This instinct, shared across mammalian life, drives us to care for and defend our young. In that sense, our usual deliberations about when to have children and how many we can afford are really assessments of our perceived ability to care for them.

Yet days like this reveal a deeper truth: we do not fully control our lives. We live in a world of data and predictions, imagining that more information will allow us to live safer, more protected lives. But data offers probabilities, not guarantees; statistics about survival as a species, not certainty for any one individual. The embryo growing inside me was already beyond my control. I could take prenatal vitamins, eat carefully, avoid risks, but I could not determine the timing of birth, the child’s health, or who this person would become.

As my belly grew and I watched my children play, I felt increasingly forward-looking and hopeful. Children do more than bring joy; they remind us of our ethical obligation, acting as a counterforce to evil. Gradually, over the following months, I internalized a different understanding of my role as a parent, not as a guardian of certainty, but as someone tasked with preparing children for life’s inevitable challenges and nurturing them in the safest world I can help create. As parents, we can teach caring and responsibility, guiding them to engage with the world in ways that reduce harm and sustain goodness. Through them, life continues, and our capacity for love and care finds its clearest expression.

A second realization emerged amid the devastation: the attacks had brought into sharp focus our human struggle with mortality. Bringing new life into the world is magical in the truest sense, a truth I had heard before giving birth, but only fully understood once I experienced it myself. In moments like these, the presence of death feels unbearable, carrying with it an overwhelming sense of helplessness and loss of control.

As the pregnancy neared its end, my husband and I turned to practical matters, preparing for a new addition to our family, though we were far less prepared for what would follow. We hadn’t planned who would be with our children if I went into labor in the middle of the night, which is exactly what happened. Still, nothing could have prepared us for what came next.

Late at night, I sat alone with my newborn daughter, BG for baby girl, whom we had not even named. At last, our small studio apartment was quiet. I had made it through another day caring for our three small children. At the same time, my husband had just lost his father, our Papi. Papi would never meet his granddaughter or share in this moment of joy. What should have been purely celebratory became something far more complex: a collision of grief and happiness, intertwined in ways I had never imagined.

It was in that moment of immense pain and profound love that I understood something with clarity: bearing children is the ultimate response to death.

item.title: What Happens When AI Does the Beginner's Work?
item.description:
Education

What Happens When AI Does the Beginner's Work?

AI is changing how beginners become professionals and how we teach them.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • AI is thinning entry-level jobs that traditionally helped graduates launch their careers.
  • Career preparation must begin during college, not after students receive their degrees.
  • Internships and apprenticeships can bridge the gap between college and a career.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

The traditional entry-level position, long a starting point for college graduates to launch their careers, is beginning to disappear. As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workforce, the entry-level career ladder that once provided new graduates with a pathway into their professions is becoming increasingly narrow.

As a result, higher education must be prepared to respond by providing students with more opportunities to gain meaningful work experience before they graduate. Whether you’re coming out with a business degree or a law degree, making that transition into a career is increasingly challenging and, in many cases, disappearing. For that reason, the college graduates of 2026 are finding it harder to kick-start their careers. It is this new reality that is pushing colleges and universities to think differently about how students move from earning a degree to beginning a career.

Colleges and universities are placing greater emphasis on the connection between academic programs and career outcomes. Career readiness is increasingly being viewed as something that should begin when students enter college rather than something addressed as graduation approaches. The California State University system's new student success framework reflects this shift, establishing a goal that every student graduate with a clear pathway to either a career or graduate school. A stronger college-to-career pathway requires more than choosing a major. Students need to understand what skills their intended careers require, connect those skills to their academic plans, and have opportunities to apply what they are learning through internships, apprenticeships, or other work experiences. Bringing academic advising and career counseling together can help students make those connections earlier in their college experience.

Source: Brooke Cagle / Unsplash

Why Work Experience During College Matters More Than Ever

While some systems are calling this holistic student development, requiring a connection between career goals and an academic plan, many institutions are recognizing that they must weave career readiness into the academic experience from orientation. In this changing environment, students are also becoming more purposeful about their goals and increasingly asking how their academic programs will prepare them for a career. AI makes this kind of planning even more important. Students already face the rising cost of college and pressure to complete their degrees on time. Many understandably want to know that the degree they are pursuing will lead somewhere. But if technology is reducing some of the entry-level opportunities that traditionally gave graduates their first foothold in a profession, what alternatives do students have?

Work experience may be one answer. Recent research suggests that gaining work experience while in college can make a meaningful difference after graduation. The Strada Education Foundation found that bachelor's degree recipients who completed a paid internship earned an average of $4,755 more during their first year after college than graduates who did not complete an internship. That finding suggests that work experience during college can do more than strengthen a resume. It can help students begin building the bridge between completing a degree and entering a career. That reality is creating a shift in higher education. The focus is no longer solely on helping students complete a degree but also on ensuring they are prepared to translate that degree into a career.

Internships and other work-based experiences are no longer simply optional additions to a college education; they are becoming an intentional part of preparing students to enter the workforce. I experienced the value of this pathway firsthand. During the final year of my undergraduate education, I participated in a year-long, college-credit internship. That experience opened the door for me to apply to and be accepted into the California State Senate Fellowship Program after graduation. The fellowship, in turn, helped launch my career, leading to my first entry-level professional position as a policy analyst.

Source: Joao Victor da Silva Ribeio / Unsplash

How Colleges Can Respond to the Disappearing Entry-Level Job

The Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce adds another dimension to this discussion by describing an increasingly uncertain pathway between education and a good job. A college degree remains important, but students may also need opportunities to develop workplace skills, professional connections, and practical experience before they graduate. Internships, apprenticeships, and other forms of work-based learning can help provide that experience and strengthen the bridge between college completion and the first meaningful career opportunity. If AI continues to change the entry-level career landscape, higher education must respond to that changing environment. Helping students earn a degree remains essential, but completion alone cannot be the only measure of success. Colleges and universities must also consider how students will translate that degree into their first meaningful career opportunity. If the traditional first job is disappearing, higher education may need to help students gain the experiences that once came with that first job before they ever leave college.

item.title: 25 Years Later, 9/11 Is Still a Collective Trauma
item.description:
Disaster Psychology

25 Years Later, 9/11 Is Still a Collective Trauma

The psychological impact and the search for healing continues decades later.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Two-and-a-half decades later, 9/11 remains a mass trauma that has a continued effect on the nation's psyche.
  • The event's shattering of our sense of safety resulted in pathologies such as PTSD, anxiety, and depression.
  • A continued search for meaning and understanding can aid in the process of healing from collective trauma.

As we prepare for the 25th anniversary of the deadliest terrorist attacks ever perpetrated on U.S. soil, we can use the lens of psychology to better understand how such an event can result in what is variously termed a “collective trauma,” a “societal trauma,” or a “mass trauma.” No matter what label we use, the events that unfolded on September 11, 2001, and all that has been stored in our collective memory since have the continued effect of being at once haunting, traumatizing, grief-ridden, difficult to fathom, and anxiety-inducing. Yet, as our yearly remembrances and tributes show, telling the story and remembering the event can help us find meaning in the tragedy, which can further our collective healing.

Collective Trauma Defined

Collective trauma may be defined as “the psychological reactions to a traumatic event that affect an entire society; it does not merely reflect an historical fact…It suggests that the tragedy is represented in the collective memory of the group, and like all forms of memory it comprises not only a reproduction of the events, but also an ongoing reconstruction of the trauma in an attempt to make sense of it” (Hirschberger, 2018). From a pathological perspective, research indicates that "people who have been exposed to trauma are at risk for development of PTSD, as well as other anxiety and mood disorders or may simply show a range of difficult emotional and behavioral responses post trauma” (APA, 2017). But what is unique about 9/11 is the fact that even those of us who were not actually present at the site of the unfolding disaster are susceptible to all the trauma responses that the research indicates are common in the aftermath of a disaster. According to Wayment (2004), “the largely symbolic threats that the attacks represented (unpredictability, possibility of war and future terrorist attacks, loss of security, threats to the ‘American way of life’) all challenged fundamental assumptions most Americans held about both national and personal invulnerability.” In essence, we are all—regardless of demographic differences—at risk of experiencing the lasting psychological effects of a collective trauma such as 9/11.

A Shattering of the Basic Fabric

On September 11, 2001, I was in the Netherlands for my study-abroad semester. One of my lasting memories, aside from the initial shock of the event itself and being far from home when it occurred, was returning to the United States in December of that year. I distinctly remember stepping into the terminal at Newark Airport into what felt like a different reality. Unlike when I had left that same airport in August, I now observed heavily armed law enforcement agents, bomb-sniffing dogs, all manner of security personnel, and a general feeling of tension and uncertainty. I can remember feeling a sense of psychological whiplash: What had been safe and normal now was anything but. According to Alexander et al. (2004), collective trauma transforms the way we “perceive the world,” and certainly my perception of the world I had known had suddenly shifted significantly.

Psychologically, we can understand this type of cataclysmic shift as jarring, frightening, and, perhaps, signifying a loss of control over our lives. As human beings, we prefer order, predictability, and safety. When this basic fabric is shattered, we are vulnerable to feelings of anxiety, fear, panic, depression, hopelessness, and other trauma-driven emotions. For many people, 9/11 was just that—a shattering of what we had believed to be a relatively safe existence.

Specific Mental Health Implications

While the concept of collective trauma is somewhat general, describing an overall response to an event, the individual experiences that occur because of a collective trauma can vary: Watson et al. (2002) point out that a disaster can result in “a wide range of psychopathology,” and though posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is the most common type of pathology experienced after a large-scale traumatic event, it is certainly not the only pathological response (Breslau et al., 1998). Because the aim of a terrorist attack, aside from creating physical destruction, is to sow fear, terror, intimidation, and mistrust, numerous aspects of the human psyche are affected (Comer & Kendall, 2007). When we feel threatened, intimidated, terrorized, and distrustful, our psychological response can take the form of generalized anxiety and panic, major depression, and substance abuse, all of which have been well-documented in the aftermath of 9/11 (New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, n.d).

Finding Meaning

This week, we are sure to see an increase in 9/11-related content on television and social media. We will see and hear stories of those who perished, heartbreaking narratives of the day, and somber remembrances of the event. This increase in content is not a morbid clinging to a tragic event but, rather, a collective effort to heal from the ongoing trauma and to find meaning in something that to this day feels so horrific and unfathomable. Psychologist and Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl first popularized the idea that retaining a sense of meaning can be helpful in surviving horrifying conditions. His seminal book, Man’s Search for Meaning, describes the search for meaning as a primary human motivation for remaining hopeful in the face of adversity (Bulman & Wortman, 1977).

A 2008 study concluded “that finding meaning plays a role in adjustment to unexpected and negative life events, such as a collective upheaval” and that “making sense of a collective adversity such as a terrorist attack is likely to foster adjustment by restoring people’s fundamental assumptions in a world that is benevolent, predictable, and meaningful” (Updegraff et al., 2008). This does not mean that we negate, diminish, or invalidate the trauma that occurred or suppress our feelings of distress but, rather, that we can, as a collective, find an understanding of a horrific event which, according to the authors of the study, “may help restore a sense of security and hasten the process of adaptation” (ibid, 2008). So, even 25 years on, our collective trauma is not forgotten, and our collective healing continues.
